title: Mixed-Effects Location Scale Models for Joint Modeling School Value-Added Effects on the Mean and Variance of Student Achievement
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological question in school effectiveness research: how to extend traditional school value-added models so that they capture not only differences in average adjusted student achievement across schools, but also differences in the variance of adjusted achievement within schools. The authors argue that standard random-intercept and random-slope models assume constant residual variance across schools, which can obscure meaningful school-to-school differences in how consistent student outcomes are.

To study this, the paper proposes using mixed-effects location scale (MELS) models, which model both the mean and the residual variance of student achievement as functions of prior achievement, student characteristics, school characteristics, and school-level random effects. The empirical application uses administrative data from London secondary schools, focusing on students who took Key Stage 2 tests in 2013 and GCSE examinations in 2018. The sample includes 71,321 students in 465 schools, and the models are estimated in Stata using Bayesian MCMC methods.

The main conclusions are that school variances in student adjusted achievement differ substantially across schools, even after adjusting for prior achievement and, in later models, student background and school characteristics. The authors also find that random slopes on prior achievement exist but explain little of the variance, and that some school types—such as converter academies, grammar schools, and religious schools—tend to show lower within-school variance after adjustment. Overall, the paper concludes that examining school variance alongside school mean value-added can provide additional insight for research and accountability, though the results should be interpreted descriptively rather than causally.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quantitative methodological/application paper using observational school census data and mixed-effects models, not an intervention evaluation. It provides correlational descriptive evidence with substantial statistical modeling, but no experimental or quasi-experimental causal identification.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has methodological significance for how school value-added and variance effects are measured in education accountability, but it does not test an instructional technology or report student intervention effects. Its practical impact is indirect and institutional rather than an educational outcome impact.
